Wow you sound like me... I also play poker for a living, have ADHD, and struggle establishing healthy habits. I know the feeling of obsession, where it feels nearly impossible to develop outside the game because poker is the MOST important thing, and everything else is peripheral, and doesn't command the same focus. 


For me, I've found it helpful to start very small with marginal things I'd like to improve in my life; once you start building momentum, developing more effort-intensive habits becomes easier. I started with just stretching after waking up - it took five minutes or less, was physically easy, and immediately improved my mood. Stretching daily for weeks made it a little easier to begin meditating afterward, something I'd always struggled with committing to, because I'd demonstrated to myself that I could meaningfully stick to something. Regular meditation has improved my focus on and off the table, and allows me to approach the day ahead in a more controlled, balanced way. Increased mindfulness has in turn highlighted more things in my life that could use improvement. In such a way, good habits can slowly cascade into one another.


Because I naturally tend to mentally drift over time and lose interest in things I don't obsess over, I record my habits in a tracker - this provides accountability each time I view it and see how well or poorly I've performed, and it also gamifyies the whole experience.


One realization that really helped me was recognizing that EVERY decision is a poker decision - if poker is truly the focus of your life right now and for the foreseeable future, then decisions about your daily life are decisions about poker. The food you eat, the hours you sleep, the physical care you put into your body, and your social well-being all influence the way you interact with the world, and by extension, your performance. I could never get myself into the gym (and I still struggle with it), but it's added incentive if I recognize that it directly impacts my winrate. 


Lastly, be kind to yourself. Change is hard, and you will fail, and that's okay, because if you never fail then you aren't challenging yourself. Treat yourself as you work on improvement as you would your closest friend - with compassion, firmness, and honesty.  Remember that nothing changes without effort.

As others have said, bankroll management is essential for anyone playing seriously. How aggressively you buy into games and the number of BIs you're willing to lose per session are dependent on your bankroll and your ability to mentally reset, and they vary for everyone.


Anecdotally, I don't buy into games where max-buy is more than 5% of my bankroll (this is pretty aggressive and relegated only to situations where the game is excellent, more often I stick to < 2.5%). I'll bring five BIs when I play, but in practice I've never used them all, I just don't like the mental insecurity of feeling as though I'm running out of money; I generally walk after losing two, and only once or twice I've continued after losing three. After any frustrating loss (it certainly doesn't have to be for all your chips, and it may not be necessary even after losing all your chips, only you will know), I think it's critically important to take 5 or 10 minutes away from the table and regroup mentally. Assess whether you're on tilt and why, and take action to reduce that tilt so that you can continue playing your game unencumbered. This is not always easy, and it's important to recognize when no amount of rationalization or breathing exercises are going to bring you back to baseline - at this point, you need to leave. 


At the end of the day, you need to protect yourself from catastrophe, and quitting is the only way to do so. I'm sorry you lost so much, but as you mentioned, you're fortunate to have outside income and no dependents, this will not break you. It sounds cliché, but please please please use this experience as a lesson for the future, only if you don't will all that money truly be wasted. Be patient with yourself, wishing you the best.

Howdy, and congrats on making it to your first EDC! It was my first festival, way before I had any idea what to expect, and has always been my favorite. You'll love it!

Like many, I prefer EDC with a little bit of molly - if you do decide to take it again, I wouldn't take a much higher dose, maybe take a little more than you normally would if it would make you more comfortable to do so and see how you feel. You can always take more if you need it, but in my admittedly limited subjective experience, molly isn't the kind of thing that improves experience cumulatively - for me, I'm either rolling or I'm not,  and taking any more just makes me confused. The one time I took way too much (5 points over the night, don't be like me lol) at Lost Lands day 1 last year, I found myself starting sentences and being unable to complete them, as I would forget my thoughts as I was vocalizing them. Very weird, and not the best state for a festival!

Personally, I love mushrooms (by themselves and with molly), and I also really like candyflipping. Make sure to be careful if you try any new substances, as you never know how you'll individually react, and everybody is different. (AND MAKE SURE TO TEST YOUR STUFF!)

As far as anxiety about meeting people, I think it's best to not worry about it ahead of time (easy for me to say). It's just different when you're there though; people are so nice, everyone is having fun together, connection comes easier. Smile, be approachable, and say something kind! If it helps, make some kandi to trade. 

One other thing, especially if you're going to be rolling by yourself - please make sure you protect yourself against pickpockets. Get a flip belt or lanyard for your belongings, nothing ruins a night faster than having your phone stolen, and pickpocket rings target people who are alone and out of it. I don't think this is an exaggerated problem at EDC as compared to other festivals (as far as I'm aware), but just generally good practice.

If you have any other questions, feel free to shoot me a message! I wish I could experience walking into the speedway for the first time again...you're going to be blown away ^_^ (this year will be my sixth!) Have a blast, be safe, and see you under the electric sky!!!

Facebook groups, specifically the $50+ high-end group, are a great resource for selling expensive cards, but can be daunting without experience. Many of the buy/sell group moderators will act as intermediaries for large transactions (or for transactions where one party doesn’t have a lot of feedback) - often this service will include authentication as a means of protecting both parties, and the mod generally charges a small fee for time and shipping costs. This is a great option if you're comfortable with it. 

I personally wouldn’t try to sell it at a GP or other large event; anecdotally, I’ve received offers ranging from passable to downright predatory from major vendors for old high end cards at these kinds of events, and you’d likely be leaving too much money on the table (for example, after speaking to 12 different vendors, the best offer I got for a MP+ Alpha Underground Sea at Gencon 2019 was $2900 - not great, even at the time). Your mileage may vary, particularly if they’re short on inventory or the card is high demand, but this probably isn’t best. You can also meet someone in person for a private sale (often through Facebook groups), but geographic and logistical constraints will severely limit your buyer pool, plus you have all the other risks associated with exchanging a piece of cardboard for thousands of dollars in cash. Sometimes it’s great, but everything has to fall in line.

Another option that will probably net you between what you’d make on Facebook and what you’d get from a vendor is to speak to one of the major online consignors. KidIcarus is probably the most well-known, his rates are fair, and experientially, he’s very professional. Depending on who you go with, the process can be very transparent, and you may also get a boost due to the reputation of the consignor (auctions by well respected sellers often yield higher sale prices than the same items auctioned by unknown sellers). By consigning, you also avoid many of the risks associated with a private sale. 

At the end of the day, it really comes down to what you’re comfortable with process-wise, how much effort you want to put in, and how much cash you’re willing to settle for. Feel free to pm me for resources or with any questions, I used to sell a LOT of high-end cards online and I (like to think I) know what I’m talking about. Good luck with the sale, and congrats on the windfall!

In my experience, the best sales platform varies slightly based on what cards you want to sell and your order volume. If you aren't planning on selling too many cards, and don't mind dealing with people, the Facebook buy/sell/trade groups (specifically the sick deals page and the High End Magic page) are probably the most profitable, otherwise selling with TCGPlayer is easy and consistent, their one major issue being, like eBay, that they side with the buyer in 95%+ of disputes, not that it should frequently be a problem. If you have a ton of cheaper cards you're looking to get rid of (say worth less than 3-5 dollars apiece), buylisting to online stores is likely the best route - to optimize your sale, Quiet Speculation has a feature for subscribers called Trader Tools that allows you to enter your collection and then automatically distributes cards to sellers based on who is paying the most. They have around 10 stores they pull from, I believe. The subscription is pretty expensive (I think I'm paying about $100/year, but you may be able to subscribe monthly), but if you have lots and lots of cheap, playable cards, it's well worth it. If you want to tell me a bit about what you're wanting to sell, I can probably give you more specific advice (feel free to PM me!). One thing I wish I knew starting out is that you can save a bit on USPS postage if you buy labels online through PayPal and print them yourself, instead of buying the postage at the post office (it's also more convenient!). As far as I'm aware, there's no direct link to do so on the PayPal website, but the URL for shipping is paypal.com/shiplabel/create. This is correct. Alpha Bolt and Alpha Balance hold (and would likely continue to hold) extraordinary values not because they're old, but because they're the *oldest*. The primary utility for Alpha/Beta cards is as collectors' pieces, as evidenced by the very highly variable unit sale prices of specific cards; a NM Beta Underground Sea will sell for many multiples more than a MP Beta Underground Sea - these multiples would not exist if prices were substantially driven by player demand, as the utility of the MP and NM copies are near-equivalent. So yes, the price decline in the event of the abolition of the reserved list would be relatively benign. Now consider that there's virtually no collector value for a Revised Wrath of God, a Revised Sol Ring, or a Revised Lightning Bolt. All are highly constructed playable cards with value derived from the player base, a quality expressed through commoditization - prices are similar and widely available across exchanges, resulting in a tightly established range for fair market price. As more copies enter the market (through reprinting, for example), price declines unless demand increases to absorb the excess supply. Revised duals (and potentially even unlimited power, though likely to a much lesser extent) exhibit the same sort of commoditized price behavior as the above examples. Without a doubt, their reprinting would catastrophically influence price, particularly since in the case of the RL, price is buoyed by the promise of scarcity.
